"A crushing defeat, no less. A dream, all a dream,"
Kondō laughed loudly from his bed in the Igakusho by Izumibashi in Kanda.
His voice rang hollow.
The folk of his home South Tama had come to visit, vegetables slung on their backs.
The Third-Month sun struck the glass window, and the room was warm enough to turn a body sour.
"For all my going the whole way out to Kōshū, the one thing I got was the tearing-open of an old wound. I never knew the Imperial army had got into Kōfu Castle so soon,"
"They say the Imperial vanguard has already come as far as Fukaya in Bushū,"
said one of them.
It was true. The Imperial staff headquarters had fixed the fifteenth of the Third Month as the day for the assault on Edo Castle.

This day was the seventh of the Third Month. Edo, too, had but a little life left in it. There Toshizō came in, his face all worn away. He had come at last, hunting down the Kondō who had fallen back beaten to Edo.
"Forgive me,"
Toshizō bowed his head.
Kanagawa, Edo, he had run in every direction begging reinforcements, but in the end had got not a single soldier.
"The defeat was my doing,"
"Come now, Toshi,"
Kondō had begun to half give up on the times.
"Even had the reinforcements come then, it was too late. The Imperial army coming up from the west had the faster legs. It was a race of legs, so there's no shame in it,"
Presently there came the Shinsengumi comrades who had scattered every which way at Hachiōji: Harada Sanosuke, Nagakura Shinpachi, Hayashi Shintarō, Maeno Gorō, Chūjō Tsunehachirō and the rest.
"We've hunted a long while for you,"
said Nagakura.
They wished to talk of rising again; Nagakura and Harada had not a trace of the weariness of defeat about them.
"Tonight, after dark, might we all gather at the mansion of Lord Ōkubo Shuzen-no-kami at Morishita in Fukagawa?"
was what Nagakura Shinpachi said.
(Well, when did Nagakura and Harada take the lead of the corps?)

Toshizō was inwardly displeased; but thinking it over, there was no corps anywhere. All of them had gone back now to being private men. And as private men, Nagakura and Harada were both of the Ōgobangumi rank, proper retainers of the Tokugawa house.
"You will come, then?"
At Nagakura's pressing, Kondō, seeming to think nothing of it, nodded, I'll come.
The two, Kondō and Toshizō, went that evening to the Ōkubo mansion. The master, Shuzen-no-kami, had until lately been a town magistrate of Kyoto, so both Kondō and Toshizō knew him well.
The gathering borrowed his study.
Five or six heads were already assembled, so Kondō, with a "well, well," took the seat of honor.
Sake and food were brought out.
About this time the former shogun Yoshinobu, secluded in the Kanei-ji at Ueno, did not even shave his pate, and held single-mindedly to a posture of penance and submission.

Hearing of much restless stirring among the war-party under him, he admonished them again and again; and the men he took to be the ringleaders of the argument for a decisive battle at Edo Castle, Enomoto Takeaki of the navy and Matsudaira Tarō of the army, he went so far as to summon, telling them, "Your words and deeds are as good as laying a blade to my own head," and so made them desist.

But the stirrings of the willing among the old shogunal retainers were not to be checked by so much as the former shogun's admonitions, and already, out of three meetings of such men held on the twelfth, the seventeenth and the twenty-first of the previous month, the Shōgitai was coming into being.
The former shogun Yoshinobu, of these stirrings among the Tokugawa vassal-band,
"lawless bravos,"
was the phrase he used (in a talk to Takahashi Deishū).
On the other hand, he was making various moves to plead with the Imperial army to call off the attack on Edo.
It was about this time, too, that Katsu Kaishū and Yamaoka Tesshū, taking up Yoshinobu's will, set about the work of appeasing the Imperial army.

By one account, it was also Katsu's contrivance that gave Kondō Isami five thousand ryō of war-funds from the shogunal treasury, lent him two cannon and five hundred small-arms to form the "Kōyō Chinbutai," and, with the fine bait of a million koku in Kōshū, sent him leaping gladly out of Edo.

"The hatred of Satsuma, Chōshū and Tosa for the Shinsengumi runs strong. So long as that lot stay within Edo prating of loyal service to the former shogun, the Imperial army's feeling will not soften. Best to drive them off,"
such, it seems, was the reasoning.

Come to think of it, the offer had been too good. That so large a sum as five thousand ryō should come out smoothly from an old shogunate ground to the last degree of want was strange; and as for the talk of "a million koku in Kōshū and so forth," both Yoshinobu and Katsu must have known full well that such a pledge would delight Kondō.

For the old shogunate the very name of the Shinsengumi was becoming a burden now. It might even be said that merely to keep Kondō and Hijikata under its wing put the Tokugawa house, Edo Castle, and even the townsfolk of Edo in unknown danger.
Though this, to be sure, is a digression.

In the ninth year of Meiji, Toshizō's elder brother Kasuya Ryōjun, his nephew Hijikata Hayato, and Kondō's adopted son Yūgorō set out to raise a monument to the two men within the precincts of Takahata Fudō (in today's Hino city); they asked Ōtsuki Bankei to compose the inscription, and the army surgeon-general Matsumoto Jun to write it out. In no long time the text and the calligraphy were ready.

Only, meaning to ask Tokugawa Yoshinobu for the seal-script characters of the monument's header, Matsumoto Jun, who had been head physician of the old shogunate, waited upon him, and when, through the steward Oguri Shōzō, he sounded out his wishes, Yoshinobu raised his face as though calling back the old days, and,
murmured the two men's names, and would say neither that he would write it nor that he would not.
When the steward Oguri pressed him again,
"Kondō, Hijikata, is it.—"
he murmured once more, and, as though it welled up choking in him, let the tears fall.

"When I laid the document (the draft of the inscription) before him just as it was, he looked at it over and over, and, in silence only, was moved to tears; and when I inquired whether he would deign to write the header or no, he gave me no word at all in answer; and when I inquired yet again thereafter, in the same way he gave me no word at all in answer,"
so it stands in a letter the steward Oguri Shōzō sent to Matsumoto Jun.
In short, however many times he was pressed, he only wept, and to the end said neither yes nor no.

To read Yoshinobu's tears: at the thought that these two, not even of hereditary shogunal stock, had worked for his sake to the very last, a human pity welled up in him past bearing. And at the same time, perhaps, there came back to him that he had driven them off to Kōshū for the needs of his submission-diplomacy.
That he refused the calligraphy was in keeping with the creed by which Yoshinobu lived after the Restoration. This man passed his whole life cut off from all dealings with the world.

The seal-script header was in the end taken on, for want of another, by the former Kyoto Protector and lord of Aizu, Matsudaira Katamori; the monument was completed in the seventh month of the twenty-first year of Meiji, and stands to this day facing south beneath an old pine in the precincts of the Fudō hall.
Now, to return to the study at the mansion of Ōkubo Shuzen-no-kami, at Morishita in Fukagawa.
Kondō's manner here struck the old officers, Nagakura and Harada, as intolerably haughty.
The truth was that Nagakura and Harada had a definite plan.

"Kondō-san, there is Haga Yoshimichi, a direct bannerman; the man keeps a Shintō Munen-ryū training hall in the precincts of the Fuyuki Benten in Fukagawa, and has many pupils. This Haga proposes by all means to join forces, form a corps, and stand against the Imperial army,"
said Nagakura.
Back in Edo, Nagakura Shinpachi was a man of truly wide acquaintance.

Come to think of it, it had been this Nagakura, and the dead Yamanami Keisuke and Tōdō Heisuke, who had ferreted out the rumor, at the close of the second year of Bunkyū, that the shogunate was to levy a corps of masterless men.

Nagakura was not only of the same school as Haga Yoshimichi of the Shoin Guard, but an old friend. Nagakura Shinpachi was a deserter from the Matsumae domain, and this Haga, too, had been a Matsumae samurai to begin with, later adopted into the hatamoto house of Haga.
"How say you, Hijikata-san?"
"Hm,"
Toshizō would give no opinion at such times. It was a habit of his. For it he was called sly.
"Kondō-san, how say you?"

and Nagakura fixed Kondō with a sharp gaze. Disband the party and Kondō was no commander nor anything else; and this Kondō, who bore himself toward mere comrades as toward retainers, Nagakura could no longer forgive.
Since coming back to Edo, Kondō,
—you are as good as my retainers.
had once let slip. By that one phrase there were several comrades of the Kyoto days who had left his following.
(So, when the new party is formed, we make Haga the center throughout, and keep Kondō and Hijikata to the standing of mere guests.)
so Nagakura and Harada were thinking.
"And this Haga, what sort of man is he?"
"A man of quality,"
Nagakura laid a pointed stress on it.
Within, Kondō had grown listless. To set to work now, at this late hour, with a man he had never laid eyes on, was heavy on his heart however he looked at it.
That mood carried over into the argument, and he let fall opinions that inclined, if anything, toward the submission party's.
"Kondō-san, I'm sorry to say it, but I've misjudged you,"
and Harada, judging this the moment of parting, rose to his feet.
"Now, now,"
Kondō calmed him, and,
"Toshi has been silent this while; what of you?"
he said. Toshizō raised his face. On his knee he was toying with a sake-cup.
"I'm going to Aizu,"
At that, they all looked at Toshizō. The idea of going to Aizu had never once entered anyone's head. Aizu was still a powerful counter-force against Satsuma and Chōshū.
"To make war in Edo is hopeless,"
"It is not hopeless,"
Harada shouted.
Toshizō turned goggling eyes on Harada, and,
"You do as you please. Here, however much war we make, I see no winning it,"
he said. He knew it from the hard sense of those days before, running about begging reinforcements.
The hereditary hatamoto had no will to fight. And those who had the will could not act to any purpose, dragged along by the former shogun's "absolute submission."
"Edo left our march to Kōshū to die. In such a place there's no getting allies,"
"Then, Hijikata-san, what will you do?"
"Nagareyama,"
"Nagareyama?"

"In Shimōsa (Chiba prefecture) it is a rich district. I know it a little. Luckily it is heaven's-domain, shogunal land; I will set up camp there, recruit troopers from the neighborhood, and once we reach two hundred, go on to Ōshū. Ōshū's hills and rivers are rugged and barren, but its soldiers are strong. The feeling against the western domains' high-handedness will run strong there too. Even should Satsuma and Chōshū take Edo Castle, before the solidarity of Ōshū they will make no headway,"
"Toshi,"
Kondō was startled.
"A grand large speech, that,"
"You think so?"
Toshizō gave the rim of his cup a sharp rub.
"But Toshi,"
"What is it,"
"Can we win?"

"Win or not win, there's no knowing till we try. Me, I don't think about winning and losing any more. I just fight while there's life in me. It seems the interesting part of my life has finally raised its curtain,"
"You've been a brawler since the days you ran wild along the Tama River,"
"Well, yes,"
Toshizō set the cup softly down, brushed off his hakama, and rose.

"Harada, Nagakura. With the times turned upside down like this, there's no going on as the old Shinsengumi. Every man has his own opinion. In the Kyoto days I crushed down everyone's opinions and threw myself into making the Shinsengumi strong. That Shinsengumi is gone. So we part,"
and he clapped Harada on the shoulder.
Harada was all at once cast down.
"Let each of us go his own road,"
Toshizō went briskly out to the entrance. Kondō came following after.
As they walked the night streets,
"Toshi, it's come back to just you and me again,"
said Kondō.
"No, there's Okita Sōji,"
"Hm, Sōji. In the end it comes to the three of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, is it. With Inoue Genzaburō, who fell at Fushimi, four,"
"But Sōji is a sick man, and Inoue is dead,"
"Then it's only you and me, after all,"
The stars were out.
Kondō laughed up at the stars with his big mouth. Back to the plain old Kondō and Hijikata of the beginning, one might say.
"By the by, Toshi, will you go to Nagareyama?"
"I'll go. You're the captain, I'm the vice-commander,"
"Will the soldiers gather, I wonder,"

Kondō seemed to have no heart for it. He had not been at Toba-Fushimi, so in Kōshū he had tasted modern war for the first time. And for Kondō it was a first defeat. Since then he had been terribly downcast.
(This man, after all, can be a hero only when he rides the tide of the times.)
Toshizō watched Kondō with an ironic eye.
"I'm a brawler, so they say, so I'll go as far as the road goes; but you, Kondō-san, if you don't like it, you needn't come,"
"No, I'll go,"

Where, but by going, was there any place of peace for him? In the mind of every staff officer of the Imperial army, now dividing into three columns and surging on like a tidal wave, there would be the wish for revenge on the old Shinsengumi.
"We go to the ends of the earth,"
Toshizō laughed with good cheer. If Edo would not fight beside them, then to go in search of a place that would, was that not, from here on, the life of himself and Kondō?
"Toshi, can't you make a haiku?"
Kondō changed the subject of a sudden.
Toshizō was silent a while, then gave a stone a light kick.
"In the Kyoto days I managed them fairly well. On official errand, the road I go out by—the spring moon,"
"Ha-ha-ha, it takes me back. The great streets and little lanes of the capital used to shudder before your sword and mine,"
"And they'll shudder yet,"
"I'd like it so,"
Kondō, too, kicked a stone. Walking side by side like this along the night road, they seemed, somehow, to go back to the feeling of their boyhood.
For some days after, Kondō stayed in Edo. Toshizō hurried to Nagareyama and made ready the camp.
Kondō gathered from the shogunal storehouses all the firearms he could, and by the hand of Asakusa Danzaemon levied laborers, formed a baggage-train, and sent it on to Nagareyama load after load.
This time, too, money came out. Two thousand ryō.
At this Kondō was moved. He felt the greatness of the hope and gratitude the Tokugawa house held toward them.
(I must do it.)
he thought.

Old troopers, too, hearing it passed along that Kondō was at the Igakusho, came, several of them. Saitō Hajime, once captain of the Third Unit, whose sword was reckoned among the finest of the Shinsengumi.
The plain trooper Nomura Risaburō, a rōnin of Osaka.
Matsumoto Sutesuke, of the same home country as Kondō and Toshizō and, besides, a distant kinsman of the Hijikata house.
These men,
"Raising the standard at Nagareyama, is it?"
said, their eyes shining.
The corps standard, too, was made ready: the single character Makoto, "Sincerity," cut in white on a ground of red woolen cloth, but badly fouled with the gunsmoke of Toba-Fushimi.
"Put that away in the wicker trunk,"
said Kondō. From here on, it was no good policy to show the Imperial army plainly that they were the Shinsengumi.
"No, let us raise it,"

said Saitō. The spirit of it was another thing. The martial show of it was another thing. Would not the Shinsengumi flag, flying at a corner outside Edo, stir the fighting blood of the men of the Kantō?
"No, no, put it away,"
On the third day they set out. Kondō on horseback. His groom was Chūsuke, with him since the Kyoto days, the second in succession from Kyūkichi, who had died at Sumizome.
Cross the Senju Great Bridge, and it was Bushū no longer. The plains of Shimōsa opened out.
Before long, the post-town of Matsudo.

From its founding the shogunate had held this a key point commanding the Mito highway, and set a guard-post here. The post-town too, a suburban settlement backed by the great market of Edo, had a population of five thousand and was a thriving place.
When Kondō came into this town, learning of it none knew when or how, the Matsudo post-officials and local folk, some fifty of them, came out to the mouth of the town to greet him.

As they took the noon meal at the inn, from the Nagareyama side, too, a welcoming crowd came thronging up, until in a moment some two hundred people overflowed the earthen floors, the eaves, and the highway.
It was, of course, by the arrangement of Toshizō, who had reached Nagareyama ahead; but Kondō, who loved a lively bustle, quite got back his spirits.
"Is Nagareyama near?"
he asked the men who had come from there, and,
"Why, it's no distance at all, sir, just there. At the camp, Naitō-sensei (Toshizō's alias) is waiting eagerly for you,"
Common country folk, but all of them in high spirits. Toshizō must have stirred them up not a little.
